title: Google Business Profile for restaurants
seoTitle: Google Business Profile for restaurants | ROAL
description: A Google Business Profile helps callers find hours, menus, and ordering details fast. Use these setup tips to keep it current.
question: How should I set up my Google Business Profile so restaurant customers can find my hours, menu, and phone number fast?
answer: A restaurant’s Google Business Profile should make it easy to call, get directions, check hours, and decide what to order. Keep the phone number correct, match your hours, add menu details, and make sure the call button reaches someone who can answer or take the order. If calls are busy, an AI phone host like ROAL can answer, quote the menu, and send pickup or delivery orders to the kitchen screen.
summary: Set up your Google Business Profile so phone calls turn into orders instead of missed opportunities.
intro:
A Google Business Profile helps a restaurant show up when nearby customers search for food, hours, or a phone number. For a busy pizza shop, deli, or takeout counter, it can be the difference between a customer calling and a customer moving on.

For a google business profile restaurant listing, the goal is simple: make the listing accurate, easy to call, and useful enough that the caller gets what they need in one try. That means your hours, address, menu info, and phone setup all need to work together.

sections.h2: What should my restaurant listing show at a glance?
sections.body:
Your listing should answer the three questions customers ask first: can I get there, is it open, and can I order now? If those answers are unclear, people often skip the call and pick another place.

Use this quick checklist for the profile itself:
- **Name:** match your real storefront name.
- **Address:** keep it exact, including suite or unit if needed.
- **Hours:** update holiday and special hours before the rush.
- **Phone number:** use the number customers already know.
- **Menu info:** add a simple menu or links to public menu pages if you have them.

A useful phone script starts before the call is even answered. If your profile says “open until 9,” but your phone goes to voicemail at 8:15, that hurts trust fast. A cleaner setup is: “Call us for pickup and delivery orders, hours, and menu questions.” That line tells the customer what they can do right away.

If you manage multiple locations, keep each one separate. A diner in one town should not show the wrong menu or the wrong number from another location. You can keep the setup organized with [multiple locations](/use-cases/multi-location) if you need different hours, menus, or phone handling by store.

sections.h2: How do I make the phone number work for orders?
sections.body:
The phone number on your profile should lead to someone who can handle the call, not just ring and ring. For many independent restaurants, that means forwarding the existing number to a line that can answer during rushes, after-hours calls, or lunch peaks.

Here is a simple owner workflow:
1. Check the number shown on your Google Business Profile.
2. Test-call it from your own phone.
3. Confirm the call reaches the right place.
4. Make sure the person or phone host can take names, items, sizes, modifiers, and ready times.
5. Update the profile if the number or routing changes.

If you use forwarding, confirm the exact code with your carrier or phone system and test it. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards all calls and *73 turns it off. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set it in the web portal. Codes vary, so always confirm and place a test call.

That matters because the profile is only useful if the call gets answered. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and the owner forwards the existing number to it, all calls or only when busy or unanswered. That keeps the restaurant’s number in place while making the call path cleaner.

sections.h2: What should a customer hear when they call from Google?
sections.body:
A call from your profile should feel fast and direct. Customers are usually calling because they want lunch, dinner, or a quick answer about hours, parking, or a dish.

A good opening line is short: “Thanks for calling, do you want to place an order, check hours, or ask about the menu?” That saves time and gets the caller to the right branch quickly.

For order calls, the host should be able to handle the details that matter in a real restaurant:
- Items and sizes
- Modifiers and notes
- Caller name and phone
- Ready time
- Pickup or delivery

A concrete example: say a customer wants two large pizzas, one half pepperoni and one plain, plus garlic knots. The host should repeat the order back, quote a ready time, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. If something is sold out, the host should not offer it. If the caller asks about a serious allergy issue, catering, complaints, or a manager, those should go to staff with a summary.

This is where an AI phone host can help. ROAL answers the restaurant’s phone, speaks the caller’s language, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, and answers questions about hours, address, parking, and the menu. It does not take card numbers over the phone; payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it.

sections.h2: How do I keep the menu, hours, and answers accurate?
sections.body:
A restaurant profile works best when the answers match the real menu and the real dining room. If your profile says you close at 10 but your kitchen stops taking orders at 9:30, callers will get frustrated.

Use a simple maintenance checklist each week:
- Compare Google hours with your posted hours.
- Check the most common menu questions: size, toppings, sides, and combo pricing.
- Review parking, pickup entrance, and delivery notes.
- Remove items that are sold out for the day.
- Test the call path after any phone or schedule change.

A practical example: if your menu says a large pie is $18, a customer can make a decision faster if the call answer includes that exact number. If your lunch special changes, update the public page first, then confirm the profile reflects it. If you have menu PDFs or menu photos, keep them readable and current.

With ROAL, the owner can paste a restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” at /try, and the system reads menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages or uploaded menus. The owner can test-call it in the browser with no sign-up needed. If the host misses a question, it lands in an inbox, and once the owner answers it, the host knows it from then on. That helps keep the profile’s phone path aligned with the real operation.

sections.h2: How should I think about cost versus missed calls?
sections.body:
A Google Business Profile can bring in good calls, but only if your phone setup can handle them. The real cost is not just the profile itself. It is what happens when a caller rings and no one can answer.

Here is a simple way to compare options using your own numbers:
- Say your average order is **$28**.
- Say you get **10 order calls a day** from your profile and phone number.
- If even a few of those calls are lost during rush, the missed revenue adds up quickly.

Now compare common ways restaurants handle calls:

| Option | Common cost pattern | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery apps | Roughly 15–30% commission per order | Extra reach, but expensive per order |
| Human answering services | Often billed per minute or per call | Simple overflow coverage |
| Monthly AI phone tools | Often about $79–$599 per location | Flat monthly budgeting |
| ROAL | $0.90 per completed phone order | Restaurants that want to pay when an order is confirmed |

ROAL has no monthly fee, setup fee, per-minute fee, or contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free. That can be easier to match with a busy profile because you only pay when a confirmed order reaches the kitchen screen. Plug in your own average ticket and call volume to see which path fits your store.

sections.h2: What should I check before I publish or change the listing?
sections.body:
Before you push changes live, run a quick owner check. This keeps the profile from sending customers into dead ends.

Pre-publish checklist:
1. Search your restaurant name and open the listing.
2. Tap the call button and make sure it reaches the right line.
3. Confirm the hours shown are current.
4. Check that the address matches your storefront and parking situation.
5. Review the menu or order instructions for outdated prices or sold-out items.
6. Make sure reservation requests, catering calls, and allergy questions have a path to staff.

A short script for staff can help too: “If a caller asks for something we can’t confirm, take a name and phone number and route it to the manager summary.” That keeps the handoff clean.

If you want a simpler setup, start with one location and one phone path. Then add more detail after you see how customers actually call. For owners who want to test the idea without changing the live line first, [build a free test host](/try) from your website, Google Maps link, or menu page. You can also review [how it works](/how-it-works) before you switch anything on the real number.

takeaways: Keep the Google listing accurate, especially hours, phone number, and address.
Make the call button reach someone who can take orders or route the caller properly.
Use menu details that match the live menu, not old prices or sold-out items.
Compare phone costs by order, not just by month, so the numbers make sense.
Test every change with a real call before busy hours start.

faq.q: What should a restaurant put on Google Business Profile?
faq.a: Put the exact business name, address, phone number, current hours, and clear menu details. For a restaurant, the most important part is making it easy to call and get an answer about ordering, hours, parking, and pickup. If the phone number or hours are wrong, customers often give up.

faq.q: Should my Google Business Profile phone number be my main restaurant number?
faq.a: It should be a number that reliably reaches someone who can answer the call. Many restaurants keep their main number and forward it when needed so the public listing stays consistent. Just test the setup after any phone or carrier change.

faq.q: How do I handle calls from Google when the restaurant is busy?
faq.a: Use a phone path that can answer overflow, take the order details, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen. ROAL can do that for pickup and delivery orders, and it can hand tricky calls to staff with a summary. That helps when the line is busy, unanswered, or after hours.

faq.q: How often should I update my Google Business Profile?
faq.a: Update it whenever hours, phone routing, menu prices, or holiday schedules change. For restaurants, even small changes matter because customers often call based on what they see online. A quick weekly check is usually enough, plus a same-day update for holidays or special events.
